body: We'd like to move to Stage 1, links to relevant documents are in the comment above.

I think I might want to see the explainer go through the known [issues](https://github.com/WICG/canvas-place-element/blob/main/QUESTIONS.md) in some more detail before moving this to [stage 1](https://whatwg.org/stages#stage1). Especially hit testing can be rather problematic (some issues mentioned in https://github.com/WICG/canvas-place-element/issues/9) and it is unclear how various APIs dealing with coordinates would work.
And also things like IME popups - since the element's layout depends on the canvas itself, it is unclear how IME related popups can position themself correctly, if the visual representation on the canvas is in totally different place.

The problem space itself is interesting. Reminds me of [mozSetImageElement](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Document/mozSetImageElement) or [drawWindow](https://searchfox.org/mozilla-central/rev/9fa446ad77af13847a7da250135fc58b1a1bd5b9/dom/webidl/CanvasRenderingContext2D.webidl#87-124).
cc @whatwg/canvas

Thanks for the feedback @smaug----. I’ve replied to the hit testing and IME popup points in https://github.com/WICG/canvas-place-element/issues/9. I’m curious to hear if the experience with `mozSetImageElement` gives us some ideas here.

That said, if I understand the stages correctly, the fact that we’re aligned that the WHATWG should explore this problem space implies we can proceed to stage 1. The questions you’re raising is exactly the kind of iteration/engagement we want to move this feature to. Stage 2 (iteration) is what would need all these issues to be resolved.
I was referring to "A comprehensive explainer " as requirement for stage 1. A bit nitpicking, I know, but there were quite a few unknowns still.

I have edited this lightly to point to https://github.com/WICG/html-in-canvas instead. https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/11588 is a (still very draft) PR for `drawHTMLElement()`, previously called just `drawElement()`, and `placeElement()` before that.
I have updated the issue description with text suggested by @progers, to better reflect the current state of things.

This API is crucial for JetBrains in developing a web-based IDE. We use it to render HTML and Markdown content, such as quick documentation popups (where documentation is provided by LSP servers in HTML format) or to display .md files. Since our UI elements are entirely drawn within a single canvas, we cannot overlay native HTML elements on top of the canvas. Popups and other tools need to be able to appear over the HTML/Markdown content, but, because everything is rendered on the same canvas, native HTML elements would always be rendered on top.
The ability to render HTML content directly into a canvas drives core features of our editor. We hope to see this API supported across browsers, as we aim to support all major browsers and currently have no viable alternatives to achieve this functionality.

Figma is very interested in using these APIs to unlock design-to-deployment workflows for complex design use cases that co-mingle HTML and WebGL/WebGPU-rendered content. We are excited to see the APIs open up more possibilities related to rendering HTML content inside our infinite canvas, and we hope to see them supported across browsers.

> ...does `drawElementImage()` just draw an image/snapshot from the element `form_element` into the canvas? Or does it clone the DOM tree of `form_element` inside the canvas? The input element seems an alive element not a static drawing.

`drawElementImage()` by itself draws a static snapshot of the element. This example is interactive because `onpaint` is called when rendering changes.

> If `form_element` is drawn twice inside the canvas at two different positions, which `drawElementImage` return should be used to update the form_element position?

The last position set will be the one that is used for hit testing / accessibility / etc. A similar issue exists with filters such as svg `<feOffset>`. We explored adding an API for setting hit test regions on canvas ([`setHitTestRegions(...)`](https://github.com/WICG/html-in-canvas/tree/d955177a448a7ce37e782c9c5dba7ed2c89a5f6e?tab=readme-ov-file#proposed-solution-layoutsubtree-drawhtmlelement-texhtmlelement2d-and-sethittestregions) that could support mapping multiple regions back to a single element, but this does not work well with features like `<select>` which need to show options relative to the dom element.

Adding this to the agenda for the WHATNOT March 19, where I'd like to request moving this to stage 2.

https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/11588 now reflects a design we believe can be implemented in Chromium, Gecko, and WebKit. In short, children of `canvas` elements are snapshotted at the end of the rendering loop, and `paint` events are fired on `canvas` where those snapshots can be used for same-frame rendering of HTML-in-Canvas.

We're also adding `OffscreenCanvas` support in https://github.com/WICG/html-in-canvas/pull/84, which I will integrate in the spec spec once some details are sorted out.

https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/11588 is now updated with `OffscreenCanvas` support. In broad strokes, the way it works is that the snapshots created during "update the rendering" get passed to `OffscreenCanvas` (potentially in a worker) and are available in the "paint" event, to draw using `drawElementImage()`. As currently defined (using "queue a global task") these would always arrive after "update the rendering" has finished so it comes with at least 1 frame of delay.
Not sure if this is a novel approach or not, but I was intrigued by the use of anchor positioning in this example: https://github.com/shuding/cobe.

Some high-level questions from a quick read of the explainer:

1. just before the `paint` event, all child elements (presumably only direct children) of the canvas are snapshotted. But in the paint callback the author may only paint one of them, so this could be wasteful.
2. Is the expectation that a page now does all its canvas painting inside the `paint` event handler, if it wants to interleave drawn elements with other canvas drawing?
3. what's the expectation if an element is painted at a larger size from the snapshot? Pixellation, or vector-based rendering? Does this need to be specified?
4. How is style resolved on canvas children? Do selectors penetrate the canvas element? Does this need CSS work, since canvas is a replaced element? This has implications on how things like `zoom` affects the rendering of canvas children.
5. "Overflowing content (both layout and ink overflow) is clipped to the element's border box". So box-shadow will get clipped in an ugly way on elements with border-radius. Would it be better to change how box decorations are rendered?
6. Are all child elements of the canvas exposed to accessibility, hit-testing etc, or only those that have been painted? What about those painted in earlier frames, and then over-drawn by canvas drawing?

> Some high-level questions from a quick read of the explainer:
> 
> 1. just before the `paint` event, all child elements (presumably only direct children) of the canvas are snapshotted. But in the paint callback the author may only paint one of them, so this could be wasteful.

This is a good point, and you're right. With the current API shape, the recommendation is to remove any canvas children that are not going to be drawn. This is actually also important to avoid those elements being hit-testable and exposed in the accessibility tree.

> 2. Is the expectation that a page now does all its canvas painting inside the `paint` event handler, if it wants to interleave drawn elements with other canvas drawing?

In short, yes. While it is possible to call `drawElementImage()` at a later time, inside the `paint` event handler is the only time when the result will not be one frame late. For cases with static non-interactive HTML, one could keep using a rAF-loop or whatever previous setup the application had.

> 3. what's the expectation if an element is painted at a larger size from the snapshot? Pixellation, or vector-based rendering? Does this need to be specified?

The [spec draft](https://whatpr.org/html/11588/canvas.html#concept-element-image-snapshot) leaves the internal representation of snapshots implementation-defined, and says it could "a bitmap or the list of commands needed to draw the element". While we could leave it that and say it's a quality-of-implementation issue, if everyone is actually using a display list we could normatively require that upscaling behaves more like browser zoom or the `zoom` property, in other words that text remains crisp, etc. (But importantly, text layout would not be done again, it's not necessarily the same as doubling the font size, as fonts typically have non-linear scaling.)

> 4. How is style resolved on canvas children? Do selectors penetrate the canvas element? Does this need CSS work, since canvas is a replaced element? This has implications on how things like `zoom` affects the rendering of canvas children.

Excellent question. Selectors should just work like in [this example's `.pie .label` selector](https://github.com/WICG/html-in-canvas/blob/main/Examples/pie-chart.html). In the [spec draft](https://whatpr.org/html/11588/rendering.html#embedded-content-rendering-rules) I've attempted to define rendering using an internal shadow tree and slotting. Since `video` elements are also replaced elements and `<video controls>` use internal shadow trees, I _think_ this won't require new CSS concepts. But if it does, we will definitely pursue it with the CSSWG. WDYT?

> 5. "Overflowing content (both layout and ink overflow) is clipped to the element's border box". So box-shadow will get clipped in an ugly way on elements with border-radius. Would it be better to change how box decorations are rendered?

@szager-chromium can you weigh in on this?

> 6. Are all child elements of the canvas exposed to accessibility, hit-testing etc, or only those that have been painted? What about those painted in earlier frames, and then over-drawn by canvas drawing?

All child elements are exposed in the accessibility tree and hit-testing. So it is important that child elements appear in the correct order (if they overlap) and that child elements that aren't rendered at all are removed, or get the `inert` attribute.

Regarding overflow clipping: the API includes "source rect" parameters for this purpose. If you specify negative top/left in your source, rect, it will include ink overflow that extends aboove and to the left of the drawn element.

For reference, here is our internal test for that scenario (if all goes well this will eventually be published to WPT):

https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/main/third_party/blink/web_tests/wpt_internal/html/canvas/drawElementImage/ink-overflow.html

One practical point about scaling: in the chromium implementation we are trying to maintain a strict invariant that if you follow certain best practices then an element drawn into a canvas should be a pixel-perfect match for the same element drawn outside the canvas. The requirements for this behavior are:

- The canvas grid (as defined by `width`/`height` attributes) is set according to `ResizeObserverEntry.devicePixelContentBoxSize` on the canvas element ([example](https://github.com/WICG/html-in-canvas?tab=readme-ov-file#basic-example)).
- The canvas context has no scaling applied at the time `drawElementImage` is called.
- The element is drawn at its intrinsic size, i.e., the optional `destWidth`/`destHeight` parameters to `drawElementImage` are omitted.

If the developer follows these guidelines, we would like to be able to guarantee that there won't be any fuzziness in the canvas rendering. If they don't, then I think it will be difficult to make a bullet-proof guarantee of "no fuzziness".

FWIW, Shopify is highly supportive of this API. One use case it solves for us is the ability to take screenshots of web components. 

This API removes the need to use things like https://github.com/bubkoo/html-to-image, which are both a drag on performance and aren't super accurate. Looking at the above library (and [similar](https://github.com/qq15725/modern-screenshot) [ones](https://github.com/tsayen/dom-to-image)), it seems like that use case has ~20K GH stars. I think it's safe to say developers want this functionality.

Three comments about the "screenshots" take:
- I previously had to use the CDP to take screenshots for things like color contrast analysis from the extension context. This could move that capability into the browser directly which could lead to faster tooling for accessibility. This also avoids one of the issues I had sending base64 images across contexts for processing in chunks (5mb limit?)--it was a pain.
- This presents a possible fingerprinting vector and, if you agree, should be noted as a security/privacy concern.
- In light of "pre-text", this presents an accurate way to measure complex DOM content for avoiding reflow. Not just for text.

@foolip 

> > 1. just before the `paint` event, all child elements (presumably only direct children) of the canvas are snapshotted. But in the paint callback the author may only paint one of them, so this could be wasteful.
> 
> This is a good point, and you're right. With the current API shape, the recommendation is to remove any canvas children that are not going to be drawn. This is actually also important to avoid those elements being hit-testable and exposed in the accessibility tree.

Hmm I don't think that's quite right. In an app where things can exist out-of-view (like Figma, Google Docs), there's an advantage to them being in the accessibility tree & searchable but avoid the overhead of snapshotting.

I guess we could have an attribute on the canvas that restricts snapshotting to a set of element IDs. It could even be the value of `layoutsubtree`.

> there's an advantage to them being in the accessibility tree & searchable but avoid the overhead of snapshotting

There is an advantage to reducing unnecessary raster work for sure. Developers can do that by not drawing content that is offscreen (assisted by the `IntersectionObserver` API, or `content-visibility:auto` on the `<canvas>` child).
@chrishtr is there a further advantage to the browser not having to produce the draw calls?

> [@chrishtr](https://github.com/chrishtr) is there a further advantage to the browser not having to produce the draw calls?

Some advantage. I think `content-visibility:auto` should already achieve that, because it by default takes into account the `transform` of the drawn canvas children when determining viewport intersection.
If it works, that seems reasonable.

A colleague pointed out that media element captions can also not be rendered using the end user preferences. (Which probably means the website cannot use canvas to render media in various jurisdictions, but also just shouldn't.)

@annevk I've made a change in https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/11588/changes/204d6aa5a477f4d770e279172c196ab241204d45 to make "User preferences for caption and subtitle selection and appearance" sensitive information. We're not committed to this however, if the WebKit team want it to work differently just let me know.

Adding agenda+ to request stage 3 for this. Here are the changes in https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/11588 since stage 2, since https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/11588/changes/71347b5565f3ec4f249640e8aac8c40de3d18b7f up to and including https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/11588/changes/204d6aa5a477f4d770e279172c196ab241204d45:

* Disallowed same-origin nesting of `<canvas>` elements since all snapshots have to be taken at a single point in time and thus cannot actually include the result of an inner `<canvas>` using HTML-in-Canvas.
* The layout, hit testing, and accessibility behavior of children of `<canvas layoutsubtree>` is now defined as extra requirements in the rendering section.
 * Sensitive information refined per above, but earlier also spelled out which CORS-cross-origin information is relevant, `iframe` and `frame`.
* Ensured that snapshots can only be used in the `<canvas>` element the child was in when snapshotted, clarified the units of `width` and `height` and that the snapshot must be updated if any of its internal state (width, height, translation, scale) no longer matches what a new snapshot would use. Importantly, this makes so that resizing a `<canvas>` will recreate all snapshots.
* Clarified that negative width and height is OK, just like in other 2D canvas APIs. (It doesn't flip the image.)
We hope to discuss this again at the WHATNOT on Thursday.
